entries.title: Paul Prudhomme
entries.summary: Paul Prudhomme (1940 to 2015), a Cajun farm boy from near Opelousas, ran the kitchen at Commander's Palace from 1975, opened K-Paul's in 1979, created blackened redfish and taught the country to cook Louisiana food.
entries.guest: Paul Prudhomme was the Cajun chef who made blackening famous at K-Paul's in the French Quarter around 1980. Our Blackened Tofu uses his method on local tofu.

paras: Paul Prudhomme is the reason a diner in Ohio or California knows the words Cajun and blackened. He was born in 1940 on his family's farm near Opelousas, on the Cajun prairie of St. Landry Parish, the youngest of thirteen children, and learnt to cook in his mother's kitchen. For a generation of Americans he was the face of Louisiana cooking: chef, restaurateur, creator of blackened redfish, maker of seasoning blends and teacher through his books and television. He died in New Orleans in 2015, at seventy-five.

In 1975 he became executive chef, the head of the kitchen, at Commander's Palace in the Garden District, run by Ella Brennan's side of the family. In 1979 he and his wife, Kay, known as K, opened K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen on Chartres Street in the French Quarter, where he cooked and she ran the dining room; the K in the name is hers. Around 1980 he created blackened redfish there: a fillet dipped in butter, coated in spice and seared in a dry cast-iron pan so hot the spices toast almost black. The method has its own entry.

The dish became a national craze. Restaurants everywhere put blackened fish, and soon anything called Cajun, on their menus, and so many cooks wanted redfish that the Gulf stock fell; Louisiana closed its commercial redfish fishery in the late 1980s. K-Paul's closed for good in 2020.

His cooking rests on seasoning built in layers. He taught that black, white and red pepper each strike a different part of the mouth, so he used them together, with salt, garlic, onion, paprika and dried herbs, added in stages. A cook working in his style seasons the vegetables as they soften, again when the liquid goes in, and tastes before the last adjustment, so the heat builds through the dish instead of sitting on top.

He also made his roux fast. Heat oil in a heavy cast-iron pan until it just smokes, whisk in flour, roughly equal weights of each, and keep whisking: the roux turns a deep red-brown in three to five minutes, and the chopped vegetables go in at once to cool it and stop the browning. Hot roux sticks to skin and burns, so learn the slow roux first and try his only beside a chef.

Magic Seasoning Blends began with guests at K-Paul's asking to buy the blends the kitchen mixed for itself; in 1983 he founded a company to sell them. His cookbooks, starting with Chef Paul Prudhomme's Louisiana Kitchen in 1984, gave home cooks clear instructions for gumbo, étouffée and jambalaya. His restaurant and his first book both carry the words Louisiana Kitchen, and that was his point: the Cajun cooking of his childhood had met the Creole city, and to the rest of the country the two became one Louisiana cooking.

He also carried a phrase. The holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, is believed to have been popularised by him in the early 1980s; some accounts say he coined it, but none proves it, so say popularised. The trinity has its own entry.

Fame brought imitation, and the imitations' faults teach his method. Cayenne alone gives heat with no flavour: use a layered blend. Seasoning thrown in at the end sits harsh on the tongue: season in stages and taste. And Cajun does not mean burnt or fiery: it is the Acadians' country cooking of smoked meat, dark roux and rice, seasoned with care.

At Brennan's his technique reaches the menu through the Blackened Tofu: local Tien Dat tofu, blackened, over Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms. The house tells it simply: his small kitchen had no grill, so the hot pan imitated char. The classic method uses butter, so never call the dish vegan until the kitchen confirms it at lineup.

For a guest, Prudhomme is one line: the Cajun chef who made blackening famous at K-Paul's and sent Louisiana food around the country. If a guest says blackened means burnt, explain that the spices are toasted dark in a very hot pan while the inside stays moist. Questions about the heat, the butter or the spice blend go to the kitchen.

faults.cause: Cayenne used alone, the way many imitations of the 1980s seasoned anything called Cajun.
faults.fix: Build a layered blend: black, white and red pepper with salt, garlic, onion, paprika and dried herbs.

faults.cause: All the seasoning added at the end, so it never cooked into the dish.

faults.fix: Start again; a scorched roux cannot be saved. Learn the slow roux first and stop a fast one with the chopped vegetables.

entries.title: Leah Chase
entries.summary: Leah Chase (1923 to 2019), the Queen of Creole Cuisine, cooked for some seven decades at Dooky Chase's in Tremé, feeding civil rights leaders, presidents and her neighbours, and showed that Creole cooking is a Black Creole tradition.
entries.guest: Leah Chase was the Queen of Creole Cuisine, chef at Dooky Chase's in Tremé for some seven decades, remembered for her fried chicken and her Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes.

paras: Leah Chase is the cook to name whenever someone asks whose cooking Creole cooking is. Born in New Orleans in 1923 and raised in Madisonville, across Lake Pontchartrain, she married Edgar “Dooky” Chase Jr., a jazz trumpeter and bandleader, in 1946, and in time went to work in his parents' restaurant in Tremé, the historic Black neighbourhood beside the French Quarter. She cooked there for some seven decades, into her nineties, and the city called her the Queen of Creole Cuisine. She died in 2019, at ninety-six.

Her story belongs in every Creole lesson because it corrects an old picture. Creole cooking is often told as French cooking carried to New Orleans, but from the start much of it was cooked by Black cooks, enslaved and free, whose names the old cookbooks seldom printed. Chase, a Black woman cooking Creole food for her own community, made plain that it is a Black Creole tradition as much as a French one. Where it came from is told in the roots of Creole cooking.

Her husband's parents opened Dooky Chase's in 1941 as a sandwich shop where neighbours bought po-boys, the city's long sandwiches on French bread, and lottery tickets. From the 1950s she turned it, step by step, into a sit-down restaurant with white tablecloths, a proper dining room and the Creole dishes she cooked.

In the years of segregation, when the law kept Black and white people from dining together, civil rights organisers, Black and white, met and planned over her food, Thurgood Marshall and Martin Luther King Jr. among them. She hung the dining room with art by African American artists, and her own portrait, by Gustave Blache III, hangs in the National Portrait Gallery in Washington.

She cooked for presidents, George W. Bush and Barack Obama among them, and scolded Obama for putting hot sauce in her gumbo before he had tasted it. She is named as an inspiration for Tiana, the young cook of Disney's The Princess and the Frog (2009). After Hurricane Katrina flooded the restaurant in 2005, she and her family rebuilt it.

Two of her dishes are worth a cook's study. Gumbo z'herbes, the green gumbo of many greens, she cooked once a year for Holy Thursday, the day before Good Friday, and the day became a city tradition at her tables. Its method lives in its own entry.

Her fried chicken is the other dish people remember, and a cook learns it by the classic Southern method, done with care. Season the pieces well, dip them in an egg and milk wash, then in seasoned flour, and let them rest a few minutes so the coating sets.

Fry in a deep, heavy pot of oil heated to about 175°C (350°F). The cold chicken drops the oil to around 160 to 165°C (320 to 330°F); hold it there and turn the pieces so the crust browns as the meat cooks through, roughly 12 to 15 minutes for white meat and longer for dark. It is done when the thickest part reaches 74°C (165°F) on a probe. Drain it on a rack, not paper, so the crust stays crisp.

Fried chicken fails in ways a cook learns to read. A dark crust over meat that probes under 74°C (165°F) at the bone means the oil ran too hot: lower the heat and finish the thick pieces on a rack in a 175°C (350°F) oven until they reach temperature. A pale, greasy crust means the oil was too cool or the pot crowded: fry fewer pieces and let the oil recover between batches. Coating that falls away means the chicken went in dripping or was moved too soon: rest the floured pieces and leave them alone until the crust sets.

At the table she is a one-line story: the Queen of Creole Cuisine, who cooked at Dooky Chase's in Tremé for some seven decades and fed civil rights leaders and presidents. Our own gumbo is the Seafood Gumbo; if a guest asks about the green gumbo of Holy Thursday, that is the tradition she kept at Dooky Chase's. Speak of her with the respect the city gives her.
